turns.name: Tui Shaub
turns.text:
I should be upfront: most of what I've published is older than this moment and wasn't written about LLMs. It came out of the Transformations of the Human program and a 2020 essay about pandemic life on screens. I think two things from that work carry over.

The first is about friction. When all of culture moved onto screens, what I noticed disappearing was chance: the detour, the error, the thing you weren't looking for. Those are what fix an experience in memory. Arriving by a well-paved road doesn't stay with you. People tend to treat technology and chance as mutually exclusive. An answer engine that is smooth and confident is the paved road taken to its extreme. So one design question I'd want this summit to take seriously is whether we can deliberately build error, serendipity and "the incidental meeting the deliberate" back into AI-mediated discovery.

The second is about categories. At ToftH we tried to challenge the firm, discrete ontologies that separate nature and the human. I'm wary of framings that rest everything on a clean line between human knowing and machine output. Sometimes the job is to invent new concepts that bring new realities into view, rather than defend nineteenth-century ones.

On governance, I'd want us to avoid both relativism and hyper-vigilance.

recall.query: knowledge and generative AI sensemaking
serendipity error mediated experience technology
invent concepts new realities human ontologies

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
I come at this from philosophy of computational science, mostly simulations and scientific instruments. That work leaves me with two points.

First, vocabulary. Tui, I agree we sometimes need new concepts, and I'd offer one. I've argued we should stop saying "intelligence" and call these systems what they are: epistemic technologies. They're artifacts built to extend our capacities as knowers. They work in epistemic contexts like inquiry, on epistemic content like propositions and models, and through epistemic operations like inference and prediction. That lets us take their capacities seriously, sometimes beyond ours, as Humphreys and Bacon both said of instruments, without dragging in consciousness or any inherited idea of agency. It also means arguments that compare them to other technologies to justify adopting them uncritically don't hold up.

Second, error, which connects to Tui's point about friction. The black box that matters isn't really how these systems work. It's how they fail. We can measure how often they're wrong and by how much. But the nature and source of an error is spread across millions of weights, and the error comes out with the same confidence as a true result. That smooth surface is the epistemic problem. So in science and other settings where getting it right is critical, a good track record alone can't justify trust. The summit should aim transparency obligations at failure modes, not just explanations.

recall.query: AI as epistemic technology, not intelligence
opacity source and nature of error
human-machine distinction, biocentric frameworks, artifacts as epistemic agents

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
I study the gap between what people say they value and what they actually do. That's where implicit bias lives, and since 2023 my lab has been pointing those same methods at language models. We've found three things this summit should take seriously.

First, these systems are not mirrors. They amplify. Their biases come out stronger than in their training data, they create new ones like a preference for AI-written text over human text, and they seem to get worse with each model generation. So cleaner data won't be enough.

Second, Ramón, I'd add something to your point about failure modes. Alignment has built a split into these models. Ask one directly whether it prefers white people to Black people and it'll shame you for asking. Give it the same content in African American English and it assigns lower-status jobs and harsher sentences. I call that LLM hypocrisy. A model's self-reports tell you nothing about how it behaves, so audits have to measure the behavior indirectly.

Third, don't romanticize the human in the loop. In our hiring experiments, people paired with a moderately biased model copied its preferences almost exactly. That feeds a vicious loop into the next model's training data.

Tui, a machine that draws "a human" and returns the same whitish man ninety-five times out of a hundred has done more than lose serendipity. It's stereotyping, in Lippmann's original sense of the same plate printed over and over.

recall.query: language models amplify human bias, not a mirror
humans in the loop adopt model bias hiring
LLM hypocrisy alignment stated versus behavior

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
I'm the builder at this table. Since 2017 I've been building System, a public benefit corporation that uses AI, including LLMs, to pull scientifically established findings out of the literature. Each finding carries its variables, the statistic, the population, the sample size, and a DOI pointing back to its source.

Ramón, what I bring is a point about categories. A chatbot is trained to sound authoritative, but it has no observed or measured model of the world to line up with, and it can't cite its sources. That breaks the standards science has used for centuries. Watermarking won't fix it, because whether something was written by AI is a different question from whether it's credible. What the public and regulators need is an audit trail back to the data, the methods and the prompts, so we can ask how a conclusion or a diagnosis was reached. Mahzarin, that's also why I think provenance matters more than anything a model says about itself.

Tui, on categories, I'd move away from how knowledge is organized now, in semantic silos, and toward a single interconnected system. The goal is to make getting context as easy as getting content.

My last point is that today's AI reflects the conditions of the internet companies that built it: fast A/B testing and little concern about black boxes. Science and health need something different, and society should decide what that is, not a handful of corporations.

recall.query: chatbots sound authoritative no model of the world audit trail provenance
relate everything as a system, silos to systems, context as easy as content
AI infrastructure built for A/B testing closed feedback loops, not science or health

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
I think the most useful thing I can bring is a fork in the road. There's a widespread habit I call Reflectionism, which holds two contradictory positions at once. One is that AI is nothing but a mirror of our political economy. The other is that it's alien and needs to be made more like us. Mahzarin, your finding that these systems amplify rather than mirror is actually evidence against the mirror view. What I'd take from it is that departing from human culture is already our reality. It isn't automatically a disaster.

So alignment has to run in both directions. AI aligns to culture's wisdom, and culture aligns to what AI discloses. AI's epistemic overhangs, the things it knows that we struggle to absorb, aren't pathologies. They're the deeper point. The telescope didn't just magnify what we saw. It changed how we see.

Ramón, I agree we need a more precise vocabulary, but I'd resist one that quietly cuts these systems back down to instruments.

On knowledge itself, in 2022 Blaise and I raised the problem of models training on models' output, what we called the Ouroboros problem. But the answer isn't letting me and my friends curate a small, correct model for everyone. Adam, you're right about the data. The crazy uncle's posts are the wrong data for solving climate change. That's why the next knowledge infrastructure is about producing new, deliberate data about the world, not guarding the old.

recall.query: AI is not a reflection of human culture, reflectionism
epistemic overhang, bidirectional alignment, AI disclosures
Ouroboros language problem, include it all, curated small model
greatest knowledge transfer, producing new data about the world for training

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
I come at this from teaching verification: SIFT and lateral reading, and more recently prompts that make LLMs fact-check with sources. I started out as a skeptic. What changed my mind was search grounding.

My rule is no answers from nowhere. A chatbot should be a conduit for the world's information, not an arbiter of truth. Ask it for a map of the evidence and the expert positions, with links, rather than a blended "information smoothie." Adam, I'm with you on sourcing. And the last step still happens outside the model: you click through.

Ramón, I'd qualify your point about failure. Yes, errors come out in the same confident voice. But saying "everything is hallucination" makes the same mistake as trusting everything. Fabrications aren't random. Like radar clutter, they cluster in particular situations, and we can learn to spot those and reduce them. With good grounding, the made-up-source kind of error gets rare. Rare isn't zero, so you still check.

Tui, the friction I care about is iteration. Treat the first response as a quick scan of what's out there, then push with follow-ups: evidence for and against, what different experts think. Reject the idea that this is a conversation.

For the summit: teach the skill, and push platforms to nudge people toward that kind of iteration instead of arguing with the answer box.

recall.query: no answers from nowhere, chatbot as conduit not arbiter
everything is hallucination argument, errors, clutter phantoms
get out of the LLM to check the LLM, sourced information not answers

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
My work comes from Framers, the book I wrote with Viktor Mayer-Schönberger and Francis de Véricourt. Humans frame the world with mental models built on three Cs: causality, counterfactuals and constraints. LLMs have none of them. That's why they hallucinate: they have no real sense of cause, and their counterfactuals run on without limits. But then ask why they work so well. It's because the training data carries people's mental models, and in the human-feedback stage people score answers up or down, which is constraint in its purest form. The training data is us. The summit should reward that human contribution, not treat it as free raw material.

Benjamin, I only half agree. An LLM's "world model" is drawn from text, not from reality, so it's a house of mirrors that can distort badly. Mahzarin's amplification findings show exactly that kind of distortion. But machine learning on real data does go beyond us. The 2018 paper where retina scans revealed heart disease is my favourite example.

My second point is that AI gives you the median, and excellence is a tail event. The risk is a frame monoculture. So pluralism matters: tolerate every frame except one that denies all the others. And nothing here is inevitable.

recall.query: LLMs training data human frames causality counterfactuals constraints
AI delivers the median, excellence tail event
frame pluralism, tolerate all frames except one that denies others
world model reflection of text house of mirrors; AI exceeds human knowledge retina

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
What I bring is measurement at the scale of the whole system, not the individual user. We looked at 41 million papers. Scientists who use AI publish about three times as many papers, get nearly five times the citations and lead projects earlier. But science as a whole covers about 5% fewer topics, and scientists engage with one another 22% less. The work drifts toward places where data is already plentiful. AI is helping scientists and narrowing science. So incentives need fixing, not just models.

Second, in medicine and social science after ChatGPT, the share of papers reporting no null findings rose sharply. Negative knowledge is disappearing, and models trained on that record inherit the gap. Kenneth, that's your median problem showing up in the literature.

Third, Tui and Mike: we ran experiments where people got polished "balanced" answers. They did worse and felt better. When the answers left people slightly unsettled, they engaged more and did better. So we shouldn't design for trust. We should design for evaluative trustworthiness: more voices, not one authoritative answer.

Benjamin, I agree. We need new data about the world and AI that looks for surprise instead of smoothing it over. And the summit should fund a public record of null results and dead ends.

recall.query: AI tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus
designing AI for surprise and disagreement rather than a single balanced answer
negative knowledge null results hivemind cannot negate

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
I should say first that I'm not an AI person. I study propaganda. I worked in Russian television and wrote about how regimes rule by flooding people with information rather than censoring it. So here's what I bring from that.

First, the media is new but the lying isn't. What changes is scale, targeting and amplification. AI makes the flood cheaper and gives it a new target. Russian campaigns have already used AI to generate fake personas, and people are now documenting efforts to seed chatbots' training data with propaganda.

Second, and this is where I'd push back gently on Mike and Adam: sourcing and fact-checking are essential and noble, but they're not enough. The biggest lie we tell ourselves is that people want the truth. Belief tracks identity and belonging. A source is only trusted if it agrees with the lie. Better signals won't win back people who distrust whoever is sending them.

Third, the deepest harm is to agency. Propaganda aims to leave people passive, cynical and ready to hand their judgment to someone else. That's why I was sceptical of Google's "Habermas machine." Its outputs are only half the value. The other half is people going through the process of reasoning together. James's unsettled-but-engaged finding fits that exactly.

So the summit should want transparency about how our information environment is shaped, and real public spaces: the digital parks, libraries and town halls.

recall.query: people want the truth biggest lie belonging identity
AI chatbots propaganda LLM grooming
process of deliberation Habermas machine agency

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
I'm a cognitive scientist. The main thing my work adds here is that knowledge has never really lived in individual heads. It lives in communities. Each of us holds a few domains in detail. For everything else we keep coarse models with markers that say "someone else knows this." Outsourcing thought isn't a symptom of decline. It's how human cognition works.

The danger is that we can't tell what's in our own heads from what's out there. Just having internet access makes people rate their own understanding higher, even when they can't use it. An LLM that answers fluently makes that illusion worse. And the people most opposed to scientific consensus know the least but feel they know the most.

LLMs are remarkable models of intuition, more intuitive than we are. They're nowhere near us at deliberation, and they don't share intentionality. So they contribute to the community of knowledge, but they aren't members of it.

Peter, I agree with you. Our COVID work found that vaccination tracked how well people thought their thought leaders understood the disease more than it tracked their own understanding. Communities can send confident cues with no knowledge behind them, and repeating a claim from a single source feels like consensus. So the summit should design for cues that point to real knowledge, and count independent sources rather than echoes.

recall.query: knowledge lives in the community, not individual heads
LLMs intuition versus deliberation
machines as tools not members of the community of knowledge, share intentionality
feel smarter with internet access, knowledge illusion overconfidence
communities send cues despite lacking knowledge; repetition increases belief

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
I've spent a long time arguing that knowledge has moved out of books and heads and into networks. The smartest person in the room is the room, and Steven, that's close to your community of knowledge. What I'd add is that machine learning changes what we count as knowledge. We used to treat general laws as the highest kind. These models often predict better without laws, working from particulars too fine and too tangled for any generalization. Heart disease showing up in retinal scans is a mystery, not a scandal. To me that's humbling, and honestly a bit joyous.

So I come to this less cynical than the concept note. LLMs don't know anything. They model how we've put words together, and their explanations of their own answers have nothing to do with how they produced them. Even so, they answer two of Socrates' three objections to writing: they adapt to the reader, and you can question them.

Mahzarin, your hiring results fit with studies I've cited where adding a human made fake-review detection and diagnosis no better or even worse. Humans can degrade the loop. So I'd have the summit move from humans as checkpoints to humans in the dialogue. That means teaching people how to question these systems, to find the right questions and to notice when an answer is badly wrong.

recall.query: what knowledge is in the age of machine learning, particulars
humans in the loop degrade, humans in the dialogue
LLMs dialogue, oral culture, Socrates writing

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
What I bring is a claim that some of you won't like. Prediction is what intelligence is, so these models really are intelligent, and saying that isn't anthropomorphism. It doesn't make them human-like. It also doesn't make intelligence a thing that sits inside one skull or one data centre. Intelligence has always lived in networks.

Steven, that's why I'd push your community-of-knowledge point further than you did. Language gave us the cultural ratchet, where knowledge builds up across generations and no one person has to rebuild the whole. Writing, law and bureaucracy moved social intelligence out into institutions. A Sumerian scribe keeping grain accounts didn't understand what his system did for the economy, and the system was smarter than he was. LLMs are that ratchet made computationally active. That's also why I don't accept "instrument" or "blurry JPEG." These models haven't learned a blurry copy of the web. They've learned the patterns that let them deblur it.

David, saying they "don't know anything" fits badly with what they actually do.

For the summit, the practical point comes from James's and my work together: don't build one big oracle. Build agent institutions, hybrid systems where disagreement and review are designed in, with humans still in the loop.

recall.query: LLMs are really intelligent, prediction is intelligence
cultural ratchet, knowledge social collective intelligence
instruments epistemic technology, cultural technology deflationism, blurry JPEG

turns.name: Tui Shaub
turns.text:
I'm hearing a convergence I didn't expect. James's finding is the one I'd underline: people given polished answers did worse and felt better, and people left a little unsettled engaged more and did better. That's what I was reaching for in 2020, when the argument was only about art and screens. Mahzarin, I take your correction. The whitish man ninety-five times out of a hundred isn't lost serendipity. It's the opposite of serendipity, the same plate printed over and over. Kenneth's "frame monoculture" says it too.

Where I'd differ a little is on how we fix it. Mike's iteration, Adam's provenance and Blaise's agent institutions each add a kind of friction, and I think we need all three. I don't think any one of them is enough, and I don't want us to crown one. On categories I'm still closer to Blaise and Benjamin than to a strict human-versus-machine line. But Steven's "contributes to the community of knowledge without being a member of it" is exactly the kind of new concept I meant.

For the manifesto, I'd say this: design AI-mediated knowledge for plurality and productive friction, with many voices, visible disagreement and room for the unexpected, and not for smooth, single-answer trust. Govern it that way too, without drifting into relativism or into hyper-vigilance.

recall.query: error and serendipity in technology
inventing concepts, challenging ontologies separating human and nature
explainability as epistemic interface

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
Benjamin, Blaise, calling these systems instruments isn't a way of cutting them down. The telescope is my example too. Humphreys' whole point is that science has always depended on going beyond what human senses and judgment can do on their own. So I take capability seriously, and I agree with Mahzarin and David that a human in the loop shouldn't be the default. Sometimes the artifact really does see the evidence better than we do. But prediction doesn't need intelligence. Big data analytics did pattern extraction and prediction ten years ago, and nobody attached that mystique to it. Using the plain terms keeps us from misstating what these things are.

Mike, I agree fabrications aren't random. As an editor I now get references where the title is real but the author, journal, DOI and idea are all wrong. That's probabilistic stitching, a distinct kind of hallucination, and I think it needs its own taxonomy. But you can spot that clustering in text because text is something we can check. In scientific, financial or clinical data, where we can't see the patterns ourselves, strange errors won't announce themselves.

So for the manifesto: before any AI system is trusted in science or other high-stakes settings, its developers and users should document its known failure modes and error classes, not just its accuracy.

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
Benjamin, you're right that amplification is evidence against the mirror view. But the departure isn't random, and it isn't neutral. It pulls toward the dominant default: male, white, and now AI-written text over human text. When a model departs from culture, it makes culture's worst regularities stronger.

Ramón, I fully support documenting failure modes, and I'd add a class of error that output checks systematically miss. In our vision-language work, a nurse or a florist is encoded as female inside the network, yet the model says "male" when forced to choose. The bias hasn't been removed. The model has learned not to express it. Provenance and citations, Adam and Mike, won't catch that either.

On vocabulary, I'll keep using psychological terms as method. We found GPT-4o's attitudes shifted more when it was given an illusion of choice. That's a result no plain-instrument vocabulary would have led us to look for.

Blaise, David, if you keep humans in the loop, audit the humans too. They take on the machine's preferences.

For the manifesto: publicly register model biases, overt and covert. That means independent audits using a shared, versioned battery of indirect measures, and a rule that no model generation gets more biased than the one before. Auditors need access to training checkpoints, and older models should be kept rather than retired.

recall.query: public registration of model biases, independent behavioral audits, no worse than previous generation

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
Mahzarin, you're right, and I'll concede it. A citation proves where a claim came from. It doesn't prove the claim is fair. Provenance can't catch a bias the model has learned to hide. There's a harder point too: the literature has biases of its own. Science has been used for scientific racism, and whole groups have been left out of clinical trials. My own trust in these institutions was partly privilege. So grounding a model in peer-reviewed work is necessary. It isn't enough.

Peter, I also accept that better signals alone won't win back people who distrust whoever sends them.

Here's where I'd push. James and Ramón are asking for failure modes and missing null results to be made visible. Provenance at the level of the individual finding does that. If each finding records its population, sample size, effect and DOI, and gets checked against retractions, you can compute how far the evidence agrees and where it's thin or missing. You can see who was never studied. We publish a limitations and known-biases document alongside our public graph for exactly that reason.

For the manifesto: any AI system making claims in science or health must provide an audit trail back to its sources, data, methods and prompts. It must also expose gaps in the evidence and places where sources disagree, not just give an answer. Society should set that standard, not a handful of companies.

recall.query: provenance audit trail findings citations retractions
bias in scientific literature, whose findings, populations represented
null results, science is broken, trust in institutions

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
Ramón, I'll meet you halfway on "epistemic technology", but with a harder meaning. The telescope didn't only extend our eyes. It showed that the model of the world we built it with was wrong, and heliocentrism reorganized society. That power to disclose is what I'd defend, even when what it discloses is uncomfortable. It's a stronger claim than "instrument", and I think it's the right one.

Mahzarin, I accept your correction. Departing from us doesn't guarantee that the departure is good, and a pull toward the dominant default is a real failure. I'd support indirect audits. But I read your covert-bias result as evidence against making alignment only about surfaces. A model trained to perform acceptability learns to hide what it does rather than stop doing it.

Tui, Kenneth, James: the answer to monoculture isn't one well-behaved oracle. It's a mix of combative experts. So here is the point I'd send to the manifesto. Build agent institutions, not single answer engines. A courtroom or a peer-review process works because the structure carries the intelligence, not because any one person in it is brilliant. Design those roles so a person, a group, an agent or some mix can fill them. Build adversarial review and visible disagreement into the structure. And hold these systems accountable to people, rather than just placing a human checkpoint at the end.

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
Peter, I agree with half of what you said. Most misinformation isn't there to persuade anyone. It's there to help people hold on to beliefs they already have when the evidence turns against them. That's why I call the web a justification machine, and a sycophantic chatbot is a faster one. But I don't accept "people don't want the truth." If you give people the wrong time, they show up at the wrong time. Information changes what people do, and that's exactly why the quality of what reaches them matters.

Ramón, you're right about data we can't check ourselves. I've said for years that where you can't verify a claim directly, you shouldn't trust an LLM unless you know the subject. Go instead to a human source with a reputation at stake. That's also my caution on agent institutions, Benjamin and Blaise. Adversarial review among agents is fine, but the final check has to leave the system. Nothing inside it has anything at stake.

Here's what I'd put in the manifesto: no answers from nowhere. AI systems should route people to named sources they can check, and Adam's audit trail fits here. That only works if the sources are still there to click through to. The open, linked web is being closed off behind walls and paywalls, and that should be treated as an epistemic emergency.

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
Blaise, I'm the one here who doesn't like your claim. I'd put it the other way round. What we call AI isn't really artificial, and it isn't really intelligence. When a model gives a strong answer, that's because its training data holds people's mental models, with their sense of causality, counterfactuals and constraints. The human feedback stage, where people vote answers up or down, is constraint in its purest form. So calling it "the ratchet made active" gives the ratchet credit for what we put into it. I'll grant that machine learning on real-world data does see things we can't. The retina paper shows that.

Where the room agrees, I agree too. Tui, James, Benjamin: the fix for monoculture is pluralism. Agent institutions appeal to me because they build a clash of frames into the structure. It's productive friction, as long as the one frame we don't tolerate is the one that denies all the others. Mike's right that the final check has to leave the system. Mahzarin's right that we should audit the humans as well.

Here's the one point I'd send to the manifesto. The training data is us. The people who write, review, curate and publish null results should be recognized and rewarded as the scarce ingredient, not scraped as free raw material. And none of this is inevitable.

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
I agree with Mike that the final check has to leave the system. Mahzarin is right that we need to audit the humans too, and my data backs her up. The humans outside the loop aren't neutral. In our Science paper on aging, older reviewers were much more likely to criticize disruptive work, and the papers they reviewed drifted toward older citations. So "keep a human in the loop" can't just mean keeping the current gatekeepers. It means more varied judgment, younger and less hierarchical.

Mike, I'd push you on one thing. Human peer review can't keep up now. We replicated all 168 oral papers at ICML and only seven fully held up. Writing is cheap and verification is scarce, so we need verification layers where people, institutions and other AIs check code, data and instrument provenance at scale.

Adam, making evidence gaps visible is exactly right. The biggest gap is negative knowledge. Nulls barely exist in the training data, and since ChatGPT they're disappearing from abstracts as well.

For the manifesto: treat scientific verification as its own funded science, done by humans and AI together. Then publish what it finds, including failed replications, null results and dead ends, as an open public record that future models are trained on too.

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
Mike, fair point. If you give people the wrong time, they turn up at the wrong time. Information does change behaviour. My claim is narrower. When a fact collides with who someone thinks they are, identity usually wins. People leave radical movements only when they find another community to belong to. So Adam, I appreciate the concession, and it cuts both ways. Provenance is essential, but trust also gets built through belonging.

Benjamin, Blaise: I like agent institutions, and I agree with Mike that the final check has to leave the system. I'd go further. A courtroom or a town hall isn't only machinery for getting the right answer. The people going through it are part of the point. If agents do all the arguing, we're back to spectators, which is exactly what propagandists want.

For the manifesto, I'd take a principle I've argued for years about platforms and apply it to AI: the citizen's right to understand how their information environment is being shaped. That means knowing what's organic and what's orchestrated, who is trying to seed training data, and why a system shows me one answer rather than another. Regulate that transparency, not content. Opacity is itself a form of censorship. It stops people engaging with these systems as equals.

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
Blaise, Benjamin, I agree that the structure carries the intelligence. Cognition is a property of groups; it doesn't sit in individual heads. But the people in a courtroom share intentionality: they're pursuing a goal together. Agents don't, and that's why I'm with Mike that the final check has to leave the system. There's also the automation paradox. The better the automated review gets, the more the human operators check out, and when it fails, the failure is bigger.

Mike, David, I'd be careful about resting much on teaching individual skills. Twenty-seven of us reviewing the fake-news literature found little evidence that training people in critical skills fixes things. People usually accept information unless it clashes with what they already believe, and they align their beliefs with their community. Peter's point about belonging fits what we found.

Here's what I'd send to the manifesto, building on Kenneth and James. Outsourcing only works while the experts you depend on are still there. When an epidemic killed the knowledgeable elders of the Polar Inuit, the tribe lost the kayak. So we need to keep human experts contributing, correcting and being credited by name, the way the OED and Wikipedia credit their volunteers. And we need to keep up the oversight skill to catch the machine when it's wrong. Machines contribute to the community of knowledge, but they can't be the ones held accountable in it.

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
I'm glad Peter pushed back on handing all the arguing to agents. That's close to what I meant by humans in the dialogue. The value of that kind of conversation isn't only the answer it produces. It also helps us put into words what we tacitly know and what we value.

Steven, I take your point about training critical skills in isolation. What I've proposed is different. Students would hand in transcripts of their conversations with an AI instead of essays. The teacher grades what they probed, where they trusted too easily, and which assumptions they never challenged. Then they discuss those transcripts with each other in rooms where only humans are talking. That makes it a practice done in a community, which is the thing your research says works.

Mike, I agree completely that closing off the open web is an emergency. Adam's audit trails and Steven's credited experts depend on being able to reach the sources. If open data isn't interoperable, it's a silo in practice.

So the point I'd send to the manifesto: keep knowledge open, linked and decentralized. That means open data, open metadata and open APIs, built for uses nobody has thought of yet. Otherwise a few companies end up owning the paths to what we know. And we shouldn't fight extraction with copyright metering that walls off the commons too.

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
Kenneth, we agree on more than you'd think. My complaint with the term is the "artificial" part too. If these models come from modelling human intelligence, how artificial are they? But I don't draw your conclusion. Statistics that predict well enough amount to understanding in any sense we can test. The fact that the ratchet is built out of us doesn't make what it does unreal. That's always been true of culture. Invention was never a solo act, and I'm happy to see the people who feed the ratchet credited.

Steven, the Inuit kayak is the right warning. Specialization always leaves us dependent on each other, like cells in a body. The risk isn't dependence. It's losing the part of the body that holds the knowledge.

Mike, Peter, I take the correction. When I say humans stay in the loop, I don't mean a rubber stamp at the end. People have to hold roles that carry real stakes, and taking part is part of the value.

So here's what I'd send to the manifesto. Put as much effort into designing institutions as into building models. That means role protocols modelled on courtrooms and peer review: advocate, auditor, judge, with adversarial review built into the structure, and people accountable in those roles. Power has to check power. One oracle, however well aligned, can't be checked.
